review: This game surprised me, it not my normal RPG or RTS, but it is surprisingly fun!  Addictive! I have it on my phone also, but playing on PC is always better.

A satisfying game. 
It's not super hard, which is by design since you can only choose between Medium and Easy levels.
There's some level grinding aspect to it if you want to fully upgrade all of your towers. Going all out isn't required, but it's a tangible reward because it improves the killing potential of your towers in a notable but not overpowered way.
I was curious about the tower defense genre, and I found this to be a fun little game that is perfect for playing 15 minutes at a time. Plus the price is so low - a great value!

11 years after the game was released, here I am revisiting it, as I only just realised I had literally missed one single Steam achievement from the game. So.... Full game reset and we go again from the very beginning, heck, why not.

This is a classic Tower Defence game, with quite nice graphics for the time. What it does is a little limited compared to some of the more modern games in the genre, but for fans of the genre who've been playing this type of game for a good 20+ years like myself, sometimes you really just want to have the game be as they once were and this game does that pretty well.

The game has a pretty steep learning curve. The first island, very simple and straightforward, more of a tutorial than anything else. But, then it gets tougher and you have to start using your noodle to make any progress. You have to think about placement, which towers work best and think carefully about your spending.

I do think that some of the more recent negative reviews may be from folks that simply aren't used to the old school tower defence style, where yes, you had limited choices and you had to make the best of them and think about where you use them and use the extras like the road blocks and mines carefully and at the right time.

Would I recommend the game still after all this time... Heck yes. The price is still really decent for the entertainment you can get from the game, provided you like Tower Defence games. I would have liked to have seen more content added, or a sequel to the game, but alas, I think that ship has long since sailed.

五种塔
一种是矿机，每张地图能布设的数量固定，最高3级；
一种BUFF塔，影响以其为中心的九宫格，可免费切换伤害、射速、范围，无升级；
一种减速塔，最高3级，没有变种，局外升级能点出毒dot；
一种物理伤害机枪塔，3级后能选高级机枪和导弹两种分支，分完能再升一级；
一种法术伤害能量塔，3级后选削甲和杀人叠攻速；
三种陷阱都不能局内升级，每局有免费次数，用完跟盖矿机共用资源
一种混凝土块，纯挡敌人攻击/行进的，局外升级解锁自然回血；
一种雷区，埋最多8个地雷，敌人经过爆炸，可以当手雷使；
一种死亡射线，在一小块区域短时间内持续造成高额伤害；
就这几种，你玩去吧，玩到后面不吐我佩服你。后面中级难度推关就是想办法摆出两个以BUFF塔为中心的塔阵挂机，甚至能做出模板来，除了开局打建筑物（保卫萝卜那种）以外基本没变数。

Ancient Planet is a tower defense game developed and published by Moonlight Mouse that aims to recapture the appeal of classic strategy titles while blending it with a colorful sci-fi aesthetic. Set on an ancient world besieged by alien forces, the player takes on the role of a commander defending the last bastions of a once-great civilization. The story is lightly sketched but serves its purpose, creating a backdrop that explains the use of futuristic weaponry and relic technologies that power the defensive towers. The tone is tongue-in-cheek at times, with a narrative delivered through brief text snippets and simple comic-like panels that add a sense of personality without ever becoming intrusive. From the start, the game positions itself as a straightforward yet polished entry in the tower defense genre, focusing on mechanical clarity and incremental challenge rather than complex storytelling or innovation.

Visually, Ancient Planet is clean, bright, and functional. The maps are presented in an isometric view, giving a clear sense of terrain and pathing, while the environments range from lush alien forests to barren deserts and metallic strongholds. The art design relies on a mix of colorful simplicity and clear readability, ensuring that enemies and towers stand out even during chaotic waves. There’s a certain charm in its cartoonish depiction of futuristic warfare, with enemies ranging from robotic scouts to hulking armored units that march steadily toward your base. The soundtrack complements the action with rhythmic, synth-heavy music that reinforces the science-fiction atmosphere without overwhelming the player’s concentration. The user interface is minimalistic and intuitive, giving quick access to tower construction, upgrades, and resource management without cluttering the screen, which helps maintain the focus on tactical decision-making.

The gameplay in Ancient Planet is where the game’s classic roots are most apparent. It follows the traditional formula of building and upgrading towers to defend against waves of enemies, but it introduces small twists to keep the player engaged. Unlike many tower defense games that restrict tower placement to fixed nodes, Ancient Planet allows you to build freely within the designated play area, giving greater flexibility to experiment with defensive layouts. The player earns resources by defeating enemies, which can be spent on constructing new towers or upgrading existing ones mid-battle. Between missions, an overarching upgrade system lets you improve towers, unlock new technologies, and strengthen your base using the gems and currency accumulated from completed stages. This persistent progression system adds depth and long-term motivation, especially since the upgrades can be reset and redistributed, allowing players to adapt their strategies as challenges evolve.

As the campaign unfolds across dozens of missions, the game gradually increases in complexity by introducing new enemy types, environmental hazards, and tower upgrades. The early levels serve as a gentle introduction, but later stages demand careful planning and efficiency in tower placement. Each map presents unique choke points and multiple enemy routes, forcing players to balance their resources between concentrated firepower and broad coverage. However, the difficulty curve can feel uneven at times. Some missions are easily cleared with basic strategies, while others spike unexpectedly, pushing players into grinding earlier stages for more upgrade currency. This pacing issue becomes more noticeable toward the later chapters, where the sense of progression slows and repetition begins to set in. The satisfaction of building powerful defenses remains, but the grind for incremental improvements may test the patience of those seeking a smoother, more balanced progression.

Mechanically, the game’s strengths lie in its simplicity and responsiveness. The controls are smooth, tower commands are executed instantly, and feedback from the battlefield is clear. Yet, this simplicity is also its limitation. While functional, Ancient Planet doesn’t take many risks or introduce new strategic layers that could differentiate it from other titles in the genre. The enemy waves, though varied in composition, often rely on sheer numbers and endurance rather than unique tactical behaviors, which can make battles feel repetitive after extended play. Still, for players who appreciate the classic satisfaction of refining tower layouts and optimizing resource flow, the experience remains consistently enjoyable. The sense of empowerment that comes from watching a meticulously arranged defense crush an invading force is timeless, and Ancient Planet delivers that in abundance.

Overall, Ancient Planet succeeds as a solid and accessible tower defense experience that embraces its traditional roots without trying to reinvent them. Its colorful visuals, flexible tower placement, and upgrade system provide enough engagement for fans of the genre, while its straightforward structure and steady pacing make it approachable for newcomers. It may lack the strategic depth or innovation of more ambitious tower defense titles, but its charm lies in its focus and consistency. It knows exactly what it wants to be—a classic, casual, and satisfying defense game with a sci-fi twist—and it achieves that with confidence. For players looking for a relaxing yet strategic experience that captures the essence of old-school tower defense games with a modern presentation, Ancient Planet remains a worthy choice despite its familiar design and mild repetition.

When I say that a game is too grind-y, that's really saying something. I have no problem with grind and meta progression, but this one's is just too slow.

As an aside, a lot of developers like to have incremental advancements that add 5 or 10% damage or attack speed or whatever (not just TD, it can be any type of game) and those are tiresome.
That's not a thumbs-down from me, just an observation.
Not every game needs to advance like Path of Exile; in fact a simple TD should probably have simple advancements that feel really powerful when you buy them. This isn't a RPG with 80 character levels and hundreds of hours of end-game grinding.
Every upgrade in a TD should be COOL. (Or at least meaningful.)

Average TD game, fine progression and difficulty but it became boring as you progress
Stage 1 to 6 boss designs are cool, each having their unique ability and somehow appealing story when you load the game
Some level designs are interesting, where you must use abilities to win instead of using towers is quite fun imo
(these stages are good for farming gems, which are essential for unlocking tower upgrades, abilities and base's perks)
Progression is fine, it does not have difficulty spike for no apparent reason

Things I don't really like:
Not much mechanic here, freeze tower is good for small troop spam if you have poison perks but the rest 
But unlocking tower's perks are quite tedious, you earn around 40-50 in early games and around 90-120 in stage 5-x to 6-x.
Tower perks are good, yet they are grindy and grinding them made the game repetitive 
Some special levels did make the game fun, the rest are a bit lame and pretty much you can win with the same strategies 
The last level is lame, the boss is just re-textured troop with much higher hp and damage resistance. 

Not really recommend this game, spend it on Gemcraft or the classic kingdom rush, these worth your cash more

Pros:
1) PC: Works on Win-10
2) Graphics pretty good
3) Enjoyable Tower Defense
4) You get 3 profiles (I assume that 3 people can play the same game on the same PC if desired)
5) Small SW install size, playable on a "toaster" (low end PC) Don't need an NVIDIA 4090 :p
------ Remember, this was released in 2015.
6) Got it on sale, so it was a GREAT value in the Steam Store

Cons:
1) In-game Clicking: To pick up coins and resources to build towers
------ This is like a mobile game, and I just don't like it.  I prefer "turn based" games where you get stages to upgrade towers.
2) Tutorial: It's ok, but it doesn't describe all aspects of the game (upgrades, etc).
------ I used YouTube videos to help with understanding the game a bit better.
3) Plot: A bit thin (and this isn't a big negative)
------ I bought this for the Tower Defense, not the plot, so this is a VERY MINOR negative.
4) Quit (on button labels)
------ This may be an English translation issue.  The word "Quit" is used in the place of "Back" at times.
------ You may want to halt the game and restart.  You hit "Quit" (which is true) but you just go back to the prior screen (so you can start again).  I guess that it simplifies the game to use the same word in various places, I don't know.
5) Screen/View: (out of visible area at times)
------ There are several battles where the "money" towers are out of view.  You need to "click the coins" to get the money to upgrade your tower, BUT, the battle is on the top of the screen, where you need to click for "gold coins" (which you use for non-tower boosts (brick walls, mines, sat laser beam, etc).  There should be a way to size the whole map so it "fits" on your monitor, versus needless scrolling.  This is just more "busy work" like clicking coins.  It can be annoying.  Maybe this similar to Con #2 (mobile style game play).

It's hard to find a good cup of coffee for less than 2 dollars these days.  I paid less than 2 dollars for this game and have had one of the most fun tower defense experiences.  Proves once again, its not about the graphics, its about the gameplay and fun, and this game has it in spades.  There are a lot of real time trade offs you have to make every level and every wave, which makes this a great tactical challenge.  You will lose often, but less than perfect wave completion still gets you progress towards macro unlocks you can choose from.  All around, a great investment of your $2
